title: ASAM: Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Scale-Invariant Learning of Deep Neural Networks
publication_status_observed: ICML 2021 (Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139, 2021); arXiv:2102.11600v3
main_claims: SAM's fixed-radius sharpness measure is sensitive to parameter re-scaling (scale-dependent), weakening its correlation with the generalization gap.
Adaptive sharpness with a normalization operator is scale-invariant and shows stronger correlation with the generalization gap than standard sharpness.
ASAM, which minimizes adaptive sharpness, consistently improves generalization performance over SAM on image classification and machine translation tasks.
methodology: The authors define adaptive sharpness using a normalization operator T_w that cancels the effect of parameter rescaling, and prove scale-invariance (Theorem 1). They derive ASAM, which uses element-wise or filter-wise normalization to define the maximization region. Correlation of adaptive vs. standard sharpness with generalization gap is measured via Kendall rank correlation across hyperparameter sweeps. ASAM is evaluated on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet (ResNet-50, WideResNet), and machine translation (Transformer).
key_results: Kendall rank correlation: standard sharpness tau=0.174 (p=2) vs. adaptive sharpness tau=0.636 (p=2) with generalization gap.
ASAM outperforms SAM on CIFAR-100 with WideResNet-28-10, achieving lower test error.
ASAM consistently improves generalization on image classification across diverse architectures (ResNets, WideResNets) and machine translation.
limitations: The paper covers only element-wise and filter-wise normalization operators; node-wise and layer-wise normalizations are discussed but excluded due to practical concerns.
Translation-dependency of sharpness for bias parameters is noted but not fully addressed.
The scale-dependency problem specifically applies to rectifier networks; the generality to other architectures is not fully explored.
relevance_to_rq: Relevant to the sam_origin and flatness_theory sub-topics: ASAM directly addresses the Dinh et al. counter-argument that sharpness can be made arbitrarily large via reparametrization without affecting generalization, which is a key limitation of the flatness explanation for SAM's OOD gains. This is important background for motivating scale-invariant sharpness measures in our study.
